items.subject: Maltese Cross Cabin
items.title: Maltese Cross Cabin in Summer
items.author: NPS Photo
items.description: The Maltese Cross Cabin, located adjacent to the South Unit Visitor Center, is open for ranger-guided tours in the summer and self-guided tours the rest of the year.

items.title: Winter at the Maltese Cross Cabin
items.author: NPS / Nathan King
items.description: Theodore Roosevelt's Maltese Cross Cabin was heated by two stoves and fueled by lignite coal readily available in the hillsides of the badlands.

items.subject: Little Missouri River
items.title: Little Mo
items.author: NPS/Laura Thomas
items.description: Take the chance to walk or camp alongside the Little Missouri. Lovingly called "Little Mo" or "Little Muddy," the Little Missouri can catch you off-guard at first site due to its northern flowing, muddy waters.

items.subject: Little Missouri River
items.title: Little Muddy
items.author: NPS/Laura Thomas
items.description: Get up close and personal with the Little Missouri River; discover why it is endearingly called "Little Muddy." items.subject: Cottonwood Campground
items.title: Pitch a Tent
items.author: NPS/Jeff Van Hooser
items.description: Whether in the designated campground (Cottonwood Campground in the South Unit of TRNP) or in the back country, take the opportunity to fully embrace the badlands by pitching your tent and staying a night or more.

items.subject: Coal vein / scoria (clinker)
items.title: Red Rock
items.author: NPS/Laura Thomas
items.description: Similar to that of a kiln baking ceramics, when a coal vein ignites (due to lightening strikes, forest fires, etc.), the heat will bake whatever rock sediment is above. Whether is be a sandstone, mudstone, and/or Bentonite clay, the layer above a burning coal seam will turn a reddish color and harde

items.subject: Coal vein / scoria (clinker)
items.title: Porcelanite
items.author: NPS Photo
items.description: Porcelanite, locally called "scoria," is essentially brick created as burning underground coal seams bake surrounding clay. True scoria is volcanic in origin.

items.subject: Coal vein / scoria (clinker)
items.title: Clinker Buttes
items.author: NPS
items.description: The bright red-orange color of clinker makes a stunning contrast in the Badlands landscape.

items.subject: Buck Hill view

items.author: NPS Photo
items.description: A view from Buck Hill, a high point in the South Unit.

items.subject: Boicourt Overlook
items.title: Winter at Boicourt Overlook
items.author: NPS / Nathan King
items.description: Snow covers the badlands in a view from Boicourt Overlook along the South Unit's 36-mile Scenic Loop Drive.

items.subject: Wind Canyon
items.title: Wind Canyon
items.author: NPS/Kim Wehner
items.description: One of the most beloved trails in the South Unit, Wind Canyon Trail, never disappoints in its views of the Little Missouri winding it's way through the forested valley of the Badlands. It also happens to be one of the best spots for sunsets, by the way!

items.subject: Wind Canyon
items.title: Sunset Perfection
items.author: NPS/Dave Bruner
items.description: One place that almost always promises a wonderful sunset view is the Wind Canyon Trail in the South Unit of TRNP. A short stroll (0.3 miles) to an overlook of the Little Missouri flowing in a curve below with badlands buttes in the horizon, the sun is the cherry on top of the gorgeous view as it set

items.description: Theodore Roosevelt National Park has the third-largest concentration of petrified wood in the United States.

items.subject: Petrified wood
items.title: Petrified Wood Hoodoo
items.author: NPS Joe Bruce
items.description: The large pillar shown here is called a hoodoo. They form when a hard caprock - in this case petrified wood - protects the softer layers underneath from erosion.

items.subject: Bison
items.title: Prairie Stroll
items.author: NPS/Jeff Zylland
items.description: Bison (Bison bison): average of 60-73 inches in height and 700-2,205 pounds in weight; primarily feed on grasses and sedges; habitat consists of a range from prairie to river valleys.

items.subject: Bison
items.title: Bison Crossing The River

items.description: A herd of bison crosses the Little Missouri river.

items.description: Wild horses in the South Unit of Theodore Roosevelt National Park.

items.subject: Wild horses
items.title: Array of Grey
items.author: NPS/Alexandria Shankweile
items.description: Feral Horse (Equus caballus): once domesticated, these horses have been living in the wild since the late 1800's. Inadvertently fencing them in when TRNP became established, the Park Service maintains the horses in their natural, feral state.

items.subject: Black-tailed prairie dog
items.title: Prairie Dog on Alert
items.author: NPS
items.description: Prairie dogs are always looking for threats. They build large mounds near their burrow entrances and stand on top of them for a better view.

items.subject: Black-tailed prairie dog
items.title: Black-tailed Prairie Dog
items.author: NPS Photo
items.description: The Black-tailed Prairie Dog lives in Theodore Roosevelt National Park.

items.subject: Elk
items.title: Fall Harem
items.author: NPS/Rolan Honeyman
items.description: Elk (Cervus canadensis): until the mating season, where males vie to protect as many females as they can (gathering their harem), male and female adult elk keeps themselves apart.

items.subject: Elk
items.title: Stoic Pose
items.author: NPS/Rolan Honeyman
items.description: Elk (Cervus canadensis): average of 7-8 feet in length and 510-710 pounds in weight; primarily feed on native grasses, forbs, and trees; habitat consists of prairie grasslands for eating at dusk and dawn, then treed coulees to rest in between during the day and night.

items.subject: Pronghorn
items.title: One of a Kind
items.author: NPS/Laura Thomas
items.description: Pronghorn (Antilocapra americana): average of 4.5 feet in length and 75-140 pounds in weight; primarily variably feed on grasses, forbs, and shrubs; habitat consists of expansive open grasslands, providing enough space for the animal to reach their greatest speed of 60 miles per hour.

items.subject: Pronghorn
items.title: Pronghorn
items.author: NPS Photo
items.description: The North American Pronghorn is the fastest land animal over a long distance.

items.subject: Mule deer
items.title: Mule Deer

items.description: Mule deer are widespread in the badlands.

items.subject: Mule deer

items.description: A mule deer buck in velvet.

items.subject: Coyote
items.title: Lonely Call
items.author: NPS/Rolan Honeyman
items.description: Coyote (Canis latrans): average of 3-4.5 feet in body length and 40 pounds in weight; primarily feed on other animals ranging from prairie dogs to deer; habitat consists of grasslands for hunting and sink holes in buttes for shelter.

items.title: The Grand View
items.author: NPS/Laura Thomas
items.description: Hike up the buttes to the left of the parking area of the Elkhorn Ranch Unit and take in the grand view encompassing the grandeur that Roosevelt found at his favorite ranching spot. One can really feel the tranquility that drew the young Roosevelt to set up his second ranching operation among the gr
